564.t: Living with the syndrome in silence
564.s: He never discussed it with other kids or his brother; his mother told him to live with it, and he criticizes how little boys are taught.
564.q: Yeah, and I went on and actually didn’t learn about until I was much older. Then when I got much older, I began to realize, something is different, because my brother – my older brother would go to the bathrooom, and I’d say, “I got to go, too.” I’d run to the bathroom. He’d shut the door. I…

564.t: Kallmann Syndrome and the clinic at Western Reserve
564.s: He and his brother were born with Kallmann Syndrome; his mother took them to the clinic and refused experimental drugs.
564.q: I was born with that. My brother was too – Kenneth – and he passed. You had to realize one thing. I felt, hey, I’m as much man as anybody else. And my mother would say, “You’re a man” and make you think the right way about being a young man. There was things that she knew you had to grow into. She…

125.t: His father's obscure origins and boyhood in Mount Sterling, Kentucky
125.s: Thompson knows little of his father's parentage, describes an orphan boyhood, tobacco picking, fights, and his father's path to teaching and preaching.
125.q: Some of these things I'll have to get from my sisters, they know a little more about this than I do because they're all older than I am and a lot of facts were kept from me. But as I said it's very important in my life that many of the facts of my family, for some reason or another, have been kept…

125.t: The stove again, a calendar and schooling in Ohio
125.s: He finishes the stove story, recalls a calendar he drew as a child that his stepmother kept, and early Ohio school years with relatives in Columbus.
125.q: Yes. To this very day I do not understand why there's not a mark on my face from this because the stove -- like I said, it was absolutely, purely red hot, as you would have to bend steel. The same -- you remember those stoves.

778.t: Her father the railroad porter and her Cherokee grandfather
778.s: Father worked as a train porter, mother stayed home with seven girls; grandmother Rachel Goodson and Cherokee grandfather who teased her to play piano.
778.q: No, just played the piano by yourself. Wasn't no band. They would sing on the stage at that time. Let me lower the mic a little, Sadie, if I can do that. Yeah, okay. You know it's not picking up too well. It picks me up fine, but then I talk too much and too loud. Yeah. By the way, you ever see one…

289.t: Stovall's family and leaving the farm
289.s: He was married 1947, divorced 1953, has sons and a daughter; he left the farm at 18 because he hated field work.
289.q: Well, I was married, I don't have any kids, I've got two doctor sons, and I have a daughter. How old are you even married for them sometimes? I got married in 53. No, I'm sorry, I got divorced in 53. I was married in 47, yeah, 47. You know, the dates basically. Yeah, 47. And I was 16. And I got the…

844.t: Mona's parents and Milt's father in Mississippi
844.s: Mona's parents moved north from Mississippi to Illinois and Ohio valuing education; story of Milt's father leaving over blackeyed peas.
844.q: Yes, well, they surprised me for my birthday last year and sent out money, I mean sent out requests that many of my friends all over the world, and asked them to make donations towards this endeavor, and they raised a lot of money and I must say that I was quite pleased to know that they had…

226.t: Raised by grandparents Carolyn and Thomas Hagen
226.s: His grandmother disciplined him and taught him domestic skills; his grandfather was a longshoreman; he gives lifespans of his parents.
226.q: Absolutely. My whole – yeah. I was closer to my grandmother – as long as she was living – than I was to my mother – my grandmother and grandfather.

492.t: Grandfather's cotton money and the sheriff
492.s: Lloyd returns to his grandfather being cheated by Memphis brokers and the sheriff warning the men who came with bats and guns.
492.q: You know... Oh! I didn’t finish talking about our men. Phew. I circle around. See I don’t take drugs, I circle around. My grandfather told those guys “I didn’t tell you to sell my stuff.” They said, “Well, we’ll bring you the money tomorrow.” You’re right. He said, “I’m selling today at these…

374.t: Learning he was adopted from Army papers
374.s: He describes his parents' unhappy marriage, finding out about the adoption from Army papers in World War II, and Daughtry's reflections on adoption then and now.
374.q: He was – when I think back on my mother and my father, they were great people. They unfortunately didn’t have a happy marriage. I think I was the neutralizing force between them. They needed a neutralizing force.

137.s: He explains finding rattlers under rocks, shooting them from a distance, and why the others flee a gunshot.
137.q: Yeah, you turn over a rock and you jump back. You know they're under there and then they'll rattle at you, too, when you're walking.

106.t: His father's job and parents born into slavery
106.s: Briggs describes his father's position in the Sanitary Department and good education, and says his parents were born slaves but never spoke of it.
106.ch: Charleston childhood and the Jenkins Orphanage
106.q: Yes, very good. He was a sanitary inspector. He was not what you would call a principal sanitary. He was under, you know, control.

378.t: Beardstown's size and the spring river floods
378.s: The town was a railroad town of 8,000-10,000; he describes levees breaking, flooded basements, weeks without heat and his mother's canned fruit floating in the cellar.
378.q: And course we have the usual problems as a kid with -- when I was a child that River would overflow and had levees around the town --

166.t: The big ranch, the bulls and the pastures
166.s: Memories of the farm and the pastures with bulls, and oil being struck on the property.
166.ch: Family background and the Tulsa music scene
166.q: Oh, let me tell you this. These romper suits, she would clean me all up and send me down to the big house to visit, you know. Well, I had to go through a pasture to get there. I'd get down to the foot of our place, it was barbed wires around it and we had a fence -- a gate there, you know. And that…

115.t: Stepfather's trade and why the family broke up
115.s: His stepfather was a shoe cobbler; he and Gus's mother separated, and she moved to Houston for better prospects.
115.ch: Childhood in Tyler, Beaumont and Houston
115.q: The only half-sister I have is in Kansas City now. That's my father's side, which is step --
